theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A small office in New Kingston needs 12 data outlets wired back to one cabinet. What should you plan first?
options: Buy the cheapest cable and connectors in bulk
Outlet positions, cable routes and cabinet layout
Which colour the patch leads will be for each desk
How many tools each trainee will take home

questions.stem: Why do you choose one colour code, T568A or T568B, for the whole site before work starts?
options: Mixing them stops power over the cable
The tester reads only one code per site
Each code needs a different cable
So every end matches the rest

questions.stem: Where should the patch panel and network switch be placed in a small office?
options: In a cool, lockable cabinet away from water
Under the kitchen sink where the pipes come in
On the floor beside the busiest desk in the room
In the ceiling void where nobody can reach them

questions.stem: Each of 12 outlets needs an average of 32 m of cable. You add 10% for service loops and waste. About how much cable is needed?
Data cable comes in 305 m boxes. The job needs about 420 m. How many boxes should be ordered?
How should you check whether a fibre optic cable is carrying light?
options: Use a power meter made for fibre
Look into the end from about 30 cm away
Touch the end to feel if it is warm
Ask a colleague to look while you watch

questions.stem: How should small off-cuts of glass fibre be cleared from the bench?
options: Brush them onto the floor and sweep up later
Pick them up with tape into a sharps tub
Blow them off the bench with compressed air
Wipe them away with a bare hand and a cloth

questions.stem: Data cables must share a trunking route with 110 V power cables. What is the safe way to do it?
options: Lay the data cables on top of the power cables
Tie them to the power cables to keep things neat
Use a separate compartment with a fixed divider
Wrap the data cables in insulating tape first

questions.stem: You must work inside a trunking where damaged 220 V cables lie next to your data cables. What must happen first?
options: Nothing, as long as you only touch the data cables
Wear cotton gloves so that you cannot get a shock
Ask a colleague to watch you while you work quickly
Isolate, lock off, tag and prove them dead

questions.stem: Why should data cables not be laid loose on ceiling tiles or light fittings?
options: Heat and weight can damage the cables
The tiles make the cables carry more data
Light fittings will read the data as it passes
Ceiling tiles turn the cable a different colour

questions.stem: A data link must run beside large motors in a factory in Spanish Town. Which cable is the best choice?
options: Unshielded Cat 5e laid on the motor frame
Screened twisted pair, earthed as the maker says
Telephone cable with two pairs in it
Speaker cable with a clear outer sheath

questions.stem: Why is Cat 6 cable often chosen instead of Cat 5e for a new office?
options: It is the only cable that fits an RJ45 plug
It needs no testing after it is terminated
It handles higher speeds and room to grow
It can share a route with power, with no gap

questions.stem: Which cable carries both the video signal and the power for a CCTV camera in one sheath?
options: Cat 3 telephone cable
Single-core earth cable
Flat twin speaker cable
Siamese coax with a power pair

questions.stem: Why is cable for outdoor runs usually a different grade from indoor cable?
options: Outdoor grade resists sun and water
Outdoor grade has fewer pairs inside it
Indoor grade cannot be put on a jack
Indoor grade is only for telephone use

questions.stem: A 50 Ω coax has been used for a TV feed instead of 75 Ω coax. What is the likely result?
options: The TV is damaged by a higher voltage
Reflections that weaken and spoil the signal
No change, as all coax is the same inside
The cable overheats at both connectors

questions.stem: A certification test fails for near-end crosstalk (NEXT) at one end of a link. What is the most likely cause?
options: The cable run is a few metres too short
The outlet faceplate is the wrong colour
Too much untwisting at that end's termination
The cable was labelled at both of its ends

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of a compression F connector over a twist-on type?
options: It needs no tool to fit it to the cable
It can be reused many times on new cables
It fits any size of coax without changing
It grips firmly and keeps water out

questions.stem: A screened twisted-pair cable goes onto a screened jack. What must be done with the cable's screen?
options: Bond it to the jack's metal body as the maker says
Cut it back and leave it loose inside the back box
Join it to one of the white-striped conductors
Fold it over the outside of the sheath and tape it

questions.stem: A balanced audio cable for a church PA system is wired to a 3-pin XLR plug. Which pin takes the screen?
options: Pin 2
Pin 1
Pin 3
The plug body only

questions.stem: Why are cables terminated on the back of a patch panel in a set order, port by port?
options: So the panel looks full even with spare ports
So the switch can learn which port is which
So cables stay tidy and each matches its label
So the shortest cables are always on the left

questions.stem: When dressing many cables into the back of a patch panel, what is good practice?
options: Pull every cable tight so that there is no slack
Use tight plastic cable ties every 50 mm
Cross the cables over each other to fill gaps
Leave neat service loops and use soft straps

questions.stem: Why must the bend radius limit be kept when dressing data cables into a cabinet?
options: Tight bends make the cable sheath change colour
Tight bends make the cable longer than planned
Tight bends upset the pairs and spoil performance
Tight bends stop the labels from being read

questions.stem: Why must data cable not be pulled with more force than the maker allows?
options: It makes the outer jacket turn white
The pairs stretch and performance drops
The cable becomes too short to reach
The tester will not read the labels

questions.stem: Why are data cables kept away from fluorescent light fittings and motors?
options: They make the cables too heavy to support
Their heat turns the cables a darker colour
They draw the data out of the nearby cables
They give off electrical noise that disturbs signals

questions.stem: What is the main difference between a simple wire-map tester and a certification tester?
options: A certifier also checks performance limits
A certifier can only be used on coaxial cables
A wire-map tester measures speed in Gb/s
There is no difference except the price

questions.stem: How does a cable tester work out the length of a cable?
options: It weighs the cable through the RJ45 plug
It times a pulse reflected from the far end
It counts the twists along each of the pairs
It reads the length marks printed on the sheath

questions.stem: A tester shows one pair as 41 m long and the other three pairs as 68 m on the same cable. What does this suggest?
options: The cable is 41 m long and the tester is faulty
Three pairs are shorted together at the far end
That pair is open (broken) about 41 m away
The cable is fine, as pairs differ in length

questions.stem: A permanent link from patch panel to outlet must not exceed 90 m. Your planned route is 96 m. What should you do?
options: Install it anyway, as 6 m makes no difference
Use thinner cable so that the signal goes faster
Use shorter patch leads at each end to make up
Re-route, or add a nearer cabinet

questions.stem: A link passes the wire map but fails insertion loss. What is the most likely cause?
options: The cable is too long or a lower grade
One end was made to the wrong colour code
Two pairs are swapped at the far end
The label is missing at the outlet end

questions.stem: Why should the tester's reference be set, as the maker says, before a day's testing?
options: So it uses less battery during the day
So readings are accurate and can be trusted
So the cables are cleaned as they are tested
So it prints the labels for each outlet

questions.stem: Coax loses 20 dB per 100 m at the TV frequency. What is the loss over 35 m?
options: 3.5 dB
5.7 dB
7 dB
20 dB

questions.stem: A 2-way splitter is added to a TV feed. About how much signal does each output lose?
options: None at all
About 1 dB
About 10 dB
About 3–4 dB

questions.stem: Why must an unused output on a TV splitter be fitted with a 75 Ω terminator?
options: To stop reflections that spoil the signal
To stop dust getting into the splitter
To make the splitter safe to touch
To let the TV find more channels

questions.stem: How should the coax connectors at an outdoor satellite dish be protected?
options: Left open so water can drain away
With weatherproof boots or tape made for it
With a coat of household paint
With grease packed inside the connector

questions.stem: Six links fail testing, and all of them end on the same patch panel. What should you check first?
options: The outlets at the desks, one at a time
The network switch's settings
The terminations on that panel
The length of every patch lead

questions.stem: A user's computer will not connect, but its link passed testing at handover. What should you check first?
options: Re-terminate both ends of the permanent link
Replace the cable all the way to the cabinet
Change the colour code used at the panel
The patch leads and the outlet connection

questions.stem: A tester reports a split pair on a new link. How do you put it right?
options: Check both ends and re-terminate to the code
Swap the patch lead at the user's desk
Cut 1 m off the cable and test again
Add a label saying the link is slow

questions.stem: Which labelling scheme is best for a building with three floors and several cabinets?
options: Numbers 1 upwards, in the order cables were pulled
Floor, cabinet, panel and port, such as 2A-03-14
The name of the person who sits at each desk
A colour sticker for each room, with no numbers

questions.stem: Why is a printed label better than a handwritten one on a patch panel?
options: It costs less than a marker pen
It can be read by the network switch
It is clear, lasts and does not smudge
It can be changed without any record

questions.stem: What should the handover pack for a new data cabling job include?
options: Only the invoice and the date of payment
The names of the trainees and their hours
Spare boxes of cable left over from the job
Test results and an as-built drawing

questions.stem: As team leader, you see a trainee untwisting 50 mm of each pair at a jack. What should you do?
options: Stop him, explain why, and have it redone
Let him finish and fix it yourself later
Tell him to tape the pairs together instead
Say nothing, as the tester may still pass it

questions.stem: How can a team leader check the quality of each trainee's terminations most fairly?
options: Look at the work of the slowest trainee only
Test every link and record who made each end
Ask the trainees to mark their own work
Check only the links that look untidy

questions.stem: The customer wants the job handed over today, but 4 links have failed testing. What should you do?
options: Hand over now and fix the four links next month
Hide the failed results from the handover pack
Tell the customer, then fix and retest first
Mark the four links as passed to save time

questions.stem: Why does a Level 3 installer follow the maker's instructions for a warranted cabling system?
options: The maker will install the outlets for free
The instructions are shorter than the drawings
The maker's cable needs no testing at all
The warranty may need approved parts and tests

questions.stem: At the end of a cabling job, what should be done with a part-used box of cable?
options: Record the length left and store it boxed
Leave it in the ceiling void for next time
Cut it into patch leads for the customer
Throw it away, as part boxes are not used

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

What do the letters STP stand for, for a data cable?
What two-word name is given to the fixed cable from the patch panel to the wall outlet, not counting patch leads?
A coax cable loses 18 dB per 100 m. What is the loss over 50 m, in dB?

What is the name of the snap-in socket module that clips into a faceplate or a modular patch panel?
What do the letters CCTV stand for?

essays.stem: A small office in Mandeville needs 12 data outlets and 2 CCTV cameras cabled back to one cabinet. Explain how you would plan the job before any cable is pulled.
essays.modelAnswer: I would read the customer's requirements and the drawing, then survey the site to fix outlet and camera positions, the cabinet position and the cable routes. The cabinet should be in a cool, dry, lockable place, and every permanent link must stay under 90 m. Routes must keep data cables apart from power cables, in separate compartments or with a gap, and away from lights and motors. I would choose the cable grade, such as Cat 6, and outdoor-grade cable for the cameras, and decide whether they use PoE or Siamese cable. I would work out the cable needed, adding about 10% for loops and waste, and list panels, jacks, faceplates, containment and labels. I would set the colour code and the labelling scheme, plan the tests and the tester, write a risk assessment, and share the tasks in the team.
markingPoints: Survey: outlet and camera positions, cabinet location, routes; links under 90 m
Segregation from power and noise sources
Cable grades chosen, including outdoor grade and camera cabling method
Quantities with an allowance; materials list
Colour code, labelling scheme, test plan, risk assessment and task sharing

essays.stem: Explain the difference between verification testing and certification testing of data links. Say what NEXT, insertion loss and length results tell you, and give a likely cause of a failure in each.
essays.modelAnswer: A verification tester checks that the link is connected correctly: the wire map shows each conductor reaches the right pin, with no opens, shorts, reversed or split pairs, and it may show length. A certification tester also measures how well the link performs at high frequencies and compares the results with the limits for its category, such as Cat 6, giving a pass or fail that can be saved for the customer. NEXT is crosstalk, where the signal on one pair leaks into another near the tester. It usually fails because too much of a pair was untwisted at a termination. Insertion loss is how much signal is lost along the link. It fails if the link is too long, the cable is a lower grade, or it has been damaged. The length result shows if the link is within 90 m; a pair that reads much shorter than the others has a break at that distance.
markingPoints: Verification: wire map and connection faults
Certification: performance measured against category limits, results saved
NEXT explained; cause: too much untwisting
Insertion loss explained; cause: too long, wrong grade or damage
Length: within 90 m; a short pair shows the distance to a break

essays.stem: A newly installed data link fails testing. Describe, step by step, how you would find and correct the fault, and what you would record.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would check the tester itself: its reference is set, the batteries are good, and the test leads or adapters are not faulty, by testing a known good lead. Then I would read the result carefully. A wire map fault shows which pins are open, shorted, reversed or split, and the length of each pair can show how far away a break is. I would check the label so I know which panel port and outlet belong to the link. Next I would look at both terminations for loose cores, wrong colours, too much untwisting or a damaged sheath, and at the cable route for kinks or crushing near the distance shown. I would re-terminate the faulty end to the colour code, keeping the twists close to the contacts, and retest. If it still fails and the cable is damaged, I would replace the cable. Finally I would record the fault, the repair and the new passing result.
markingPoints: Checks the tester and leads first
Reads the result type and the distance to the fault
Identifies the link by its labels and inspects both terminations and the route
Re-terminates or replaces the cable correctly, then retests
Records the fault, repair and final result

essays.stem: Explain how electrical noise can affect signal and data cables, and describe the ways an installer reduces it.
essays.modelAnswer: Electrical noise is unwanted voltage picked up from nearby power cables, motors, fluorescent lights, welders or radio transmitters. It can cause data errors, slow networks, humming in audio systems and lines on CCTV pictures. Installers reduce it in several ways. Twisted pairs cancel much of the noise, so the twists must be kept up to the terminations. Data cables are kept apart from power cables, in separate compartments or at a set distance, and where they must cross, they cross at a right angle. Screened cable is used near heavy noise sources, and its screen is terminated and earthed exactly as the maker or drawing says, because a poorly earthed screen can make things worse. Balanced audio lines are used for long microphone runs. Cables are routed away from lights and motors, and good quality connectors are fitted correctly.
markingPoints: Sources of noise and their effects on data, audio and video
Twisting cancels noise; keep twists to the termination
Separation from power; crossing at a right angle
Screened cable with the screen terminated and earthed as specified
Balanced lines and routing away from noise sources

essays.stem: You lead a team terminating 24 cables onto a patch panel in a wall cabinet. Describe how you would organise the work so the result is neat, correct and easy to maintain.
essays.modelAnswer: Before starting I would check that every cable is labelled at the cabinet end and agree the port order with the labelling plan. I would mount the panel and a cable manager, and bring the cables in from one side in a neat bundle, leaving a service loop, then fan them out to their ports in order. I would make sure bend radius limits are kept and use soft hook-and-loop straps, not tight plastic ties. Each cable would be stripped only as far as needed, the pairs kept twisted to the contacts, and punched down to the colour code on the panel. I would share the ports between team members, record who terminated each, and check the first few of each person's work before they continue. When all are done, I would fit the printed port labels, test every link, and leave the cabinet clean with good airflow.
markingPoints: Checks labels and port order before starting
Neat dressing: service loop, bend radius, soft straps, cable manager
Correct termination: short strip, twists kept, colour code followed
Shares and records the work; checks each person's early terminations
Labels, tests every link, leaves the cabinet tidy and ventilated

essays.stem: A guest house in Port Antonio wants one satellite or aerial feed split to four TV outlets. Explain how you would plan and terminate the coax system so every TV gets a good signal.
essays.modelAnswer: I would use 75 Ω coax of good quality, such as RG6, with outdoor grade for the part outside. I would plan the cable runs to keep them as short as possible, because coax loses signal with length. For example, at 20 dB per 100 m, a 30 m run loses 6 dB. A 4-way splitter loses roughly 7–8 dB at each output, so I would add up the cable loss and the splitter loss to check the signal will still be strong enough, and plan an amplifier if it will not. I would fit compression F connectors with the right tool, with the centre conductor cut to the length the maker says and no braid touching it. Any unused splitter output gets a 75 Ω terminator. Outdoor connectors get weatherproof boots, and the cable has a drip loop. I would test each outlet with a signal meter if available, label each run, and record the results.
markingPoints: 75 Ω coax of suitable grade, outdoor grade outside
Works out cable and splitter losses and plans an amplifier if needed
Correct compression F connectors with the right tool
Terminators on unused outputs; weatherproofing and drip loops
Tests each outlet, labels and records

essays.stem: Compare using Siamese coax cable and using twisted-pair data cable with PoE for a new set of CCTV cameras at a shop. Which would you recommend, and why?
essays.modelAnswer: Siamese cable has a coax for the video and a pair of conductors for power in one sheath. It suits analogue or HD-over-coax cameras and a recorder with coax inputs. The video and power each need their own connectors, often BNC for video and a DC plug for power, and the power supply sits at the recorder end. Twisted-pair cable with PoE carries both data and power on one cable to IP cameras, using RJ45 connectors and a PoE switch or recorder. It is simpler to terminate and test with standard data tools, but each run must stay within about 100 m. For a new system I would usually recommend IP cameras on PoE because one cable does both jobs, it fits the shop's network, and the cameras can be upgraded. If the shop already has a coax recorder, Siamese cable may be cheaper. Either way, outdoor runs need outdoor-grade cable.
markingPoints: Describes Siamese cable: coax plus power pair, BNC and DC connectors, separate power supply
Describes PoE: data and power on one twisted-pair cable, RJ45, PoE switch or recorder
Notes the length limit for PoE runs
Makes a clear recommendation with reasons linked to the shop's equipment
Mentions outdoor-grade cable for outside runs

essays.stem: You supervise three trainees terminating data outlets on a job. Describe how you would make sure their work is of good quality, and what records you would keep.
essays.modelAnswer: Before they start, I would show the method once: strip length, keeping the twists, following the colour code on the jack, and the right tools. I would give each trainee a set of outlets and record which ones are theirs. I would watch each person's first two terminations closely and check them before they carry on, then check at intervals. Faults such as too much untwisting, nicked cores or loose sheath grip would be pointed out at once, explained, and redone. Every link would be tested with the tester, and the results saved with the link label. Where a link fails, the trainee who made it would find and fix the fault with my help, then retest. I would keep the test results, a record of faults found and who made them, and notes on any extra training each trainee needs.
markingPoints: Demonstrates the method and standard before work starts
Allocates and records who terminates which outlets
Checks early work and at intervals; corrects faults with explanation
Tests every link and has failures fixed and retested
Keeps test results, fault records and training notes

essays.stem: Describe the hazards on a signal and data cabling job in an occupied office building, and the controls you would put in place.
essays.modelAnswer: Working in ceiling voids and on ladders can lead to falls, so I would use podium steps or a tower that are checked and set up correctly, and never stand on ceiling tiles. Ceiling voids can be hot and dusty and hide sharp edges, so we would use lighting, gloves and dust masks, and take breaks. Power cables may share routes with our cables. If we must work where power cables are damaged or exposed, those circuits must be isolated, locked off, tagged and proved dead with a tester checked before and after use. Fibre off-cuts are sharp and go into a sharps tub, and nobody looks into a fibre end. PoE cables carry power, so they are unplugged before re-termination. In an occupied office, cables on the floor are trip hazards, so the work area is cordoned off and kept tidy, and staff are told about our work.
markingPoints: Work at height: suitable access equipment, not standing on ceiling tiles
Ceiling voids: heat, dust and sharp edges controlled
Power cables: full safe isolation where needed, with the tester checked before and after
Fibre and PoE hazards controlled
Occupied building: trip hazards, cordons and informing staff

essays.stem: Explain why labelling and handover records matter for signal and data cabling, and describe a good handover pack for a customer.
essays.modelAnswer: Good labels let anyone find the right cable quickly, at the outlet and at the panel, without tracing or guessing. This saves time when moving users, adding equipment or finding faults, and stops people unplugging the wrong link. Records show that every link was tested and passed when it was handed over, which protects both the installer and the customer, and they may be needed for a maker's warranty. A good handover pack has a floor plan or as-built drawing showing every outlet and its label, the labelling scheme explained, the test results for every link with the date and the tester used, a list of the cable and components installed, the cabinet layout, and any links that are spare or have known limits. It also gives contact details for support. The pack is given in print and in an electronic copy.
markingPoints: Labels make tracing, moves and fault-finding quick and safe
Records prove the system was tested and passed; may support a warranty
As-built drawing with every outlet label and the labelling scheme
Test results with date and tester; components list and cabinet layout
Spare links, contacts, and copies in print and electronic form

practical1.title: Install, terminate, test and document a small structured cabling system
practical1.brief: On a training bay, the group installs a small data system for an imaginary office: a wall cabinet with a 12-port (or larger) patch panel and cable manager, and six data outlets fed from it. First, plan the job together: mark the outlet positions, agree the colour code (T568A or T568B) and write a labelling scheme. Then run and dress the cables, leaving service loops. Each member terminates at least one outlet and at least one patch panel port while the assessor watches, and records which ones they made. One member at a time acts as team leader and checks another member's terminations before they are closed up. Test every link with the Centre's tester and save or write down each result. Find and fix any failures, then retest. Finish by fitting printed labels and drawing a simple as-built layout. Photograph each stage and hand in the plan, the test results and the as-built layout.
materials: Wall cabinet or training frame, 12-port patch panel and cable manager
Six data outlets (faceplates and keystone jacks) and back boxes or surface boxes
Punch-down tool, cable stripper, side cutters
Cable tester (a certification tester if the Centre has one; otherwise a wire-map and length tester)
Hook-and-loop straps, label printer or printed labels
Plan sheet, labelling scheme form and test record sheet
Safety glasses, and steps that meet the Centre's rules
photos: The plan with the outlet positions and labelling scheme
Cables dressed into the cabinet with service loops
A close-up of a terminated patch panel port with the twists kept
A close-up of a terminated outlet jack
The tester connected to a link, showing a result
The labelled patch panel and outlets
The test record and as-built layout
checklist: Followed the agreed colour code without error
Stripped the sheath only as far as needed and kept pair twists to the contacts
Dressed cables neatly, with service loops and no tight bends or crushed ties
Checked another member's work fairly as team leader
Tested links correctly and recorded results accurately
Found and fixed any fault in their own work, then retested
Labelled to the agreed scheme and helped with the as-built layout
safety: No mains supply is used on the bay
Wear safety glasses when cutting and trimming conductors
Use steps or ladders only as the Centre's rules allow
Pick up off-cuts as you go so nobody slips or steps on them

practical2.title: Terminate coax and audio cables, and diagnose faulty leads
practical2.brief: Part A: the group builds a small TV distribution on a board: one feed into a 4-way splitter and four coax runs to outlets, fitting compression F connectors, a 75 Ω terminator on any unused port, and labelling each run. Work out the expected signal loss to each outlet using the cable and splitter figures the assessor gives, and test each run for continuity and shorts (and with a signal meter if the Centre has one). Part B: each member makes one balanced audio lead with 3-pin XLR plugs and one screened multi-core signal cable to screw terminals with ferrules, and tests them. Part C: the assessor gives the group six faulty leads (data, coax and audio). The group tests each one, writes down the fault and where it is, repairs it, retests it, and fills in a fault report. Each member diagnoses at least one lead and explains the fault to the assessor. Photograph each stage and hand in the loss sums, the test results and the fault report.
materials: RG6 (75 Ω) coax, compression F connectors and compression tool, coax stripper
4-way splitter, 75 Ω terminators, four coax outlets on a board
Balanced audio cable and 3-pin XLR plugs, soldering iron and stand (if the plugs are solder type)
Screened multi-core signal cable, a terminal strip and bootlace ferrules with crimp tool
Multimeter or continuity tester, data cable tester, signal meter if available
Six faulty leads prepared by the assessor
Loss calculation sheet, test record and fault report forms
photos: The coax distribution board with the splitter, terminator and labels
A close-up of a fitted compression F connector
A finished XLR lead with the plug open, showing the pin connections
The screened cable terminated with ferrules on the terminal strip
A faulty lead being tested, with the result shown
checklist: Fitted F connectors correctly: centre conductor to length, no braid touching it, firmly compressed
Fitted a terminator to every unused splitter port and labelled each run
Worked out the expected losses correctly
Wired the XLR lead with the screen on pin 1 and the signal pins the same at both ends
Terminated the screened cable neatly with ferrules and the screen as the drawing says
Diagnosed a faulty lead with the right test and explained the fault
Repaired and retested the lead, and recorded it on the fault report
safety: No mains supply is used; the boards and leads are dead
If soldering, use the iron in its stand, with fume extraction or good airflow, and wash your hands after
Wear safety glasses when cutting conductors and braid
Keep blades and cutters closed or covered when not in use
